lesson.title: Running Totals: Cumulative Frequency and What Percent Falls Below
lesson.summary: Cumulative frequency tracks a running total of counts up to and including each value in an ordered data set, answering how many individuals fall at or below a given point.
lesson.body:
Cumulative frequency answers a different kind of question than a plain frequency table does. Instead of asking how many individuals had exactly this value, it asks how many individuals had this value or lower. The cumulative frequency for any row in an ordered table is the running total of that row's frequency plus every frequency above it, so it only makes sense when the categories or values can be meaningfully ordered from lowest to highest, which is why cumulative frequency is used mainly with quantitative data or ordered categorical data like letter grades.

To build a cumulative frequency column, arrange the values from smallest to largest, then add each frequency to the running sum of all frequencies before it. Cumulative relative frequency works the same way but uses relative frequencies, or equivalently divides each cumulative frequency by the total sample size, giving the proportion of individuals at or below each value.

Consider 25 students who took a quiz scored out of 10 points, with scores of 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 only. The frequency table is: score 6, frequency 3. Score 7, frequency 6. Score 8, frequency 9. Score 9, frequency 5. Score 10, frequency 2. Check the total: 3 plus 6 plus 9 plus 5 plus 2 equals 25, matching the class size.

The cumulative frequency column is built by running totals. At score 6, the cumulative frequency is just 3. At score 7, it is 3 plus 6, which equals 9. At score 8, it is 9 plus 9, which equals 18. At score 9, it is 18 plus 5, which equals 23. At score 10, it is 23 plus 2, which equals 25, the full class, as it must be, since every student scored 10 or below. Converting to cumulative relative frequency by dividing by 25: score 6 gives 3 divided by 25 equals 0.12, score 7 gives 9 divided by 25 equals 0.36, score 8 gives 18 divided by 25 equals 0.72, score 9 gives 23 divided by 25 equals 0.92, and score 10 gives 25 divided by 25 equals 1.00.

That 0.72 value has a direct, useful interpretation: 72 percent of the class scored an 8 or lower on the quiz, which also means 28 percent scored a 9 or a 10. This kind of statement, describing what fraction of a group falls at or below a certain point, is exactly the reasoning behind percentiles, and cumulative relative frequency graphs, often called ogives, are drawn by plotting these running proportions against the values, producing a rising curve that never decreases as it moves from left to right.

It is important not to confuse a plain relative frequency with a cumulative relative frequency, since the two answer different questions. The plain relative frequency for score 8 alone was 9 divided by 25, which equals 0.36, describing only the 36 percent of students who scored exactly an 8. The cumulative relative frequency at score 8, however, was 0.72, because it also folds in every student who scored a 6 or a 7. Both numbers are correct and both are useful, but plain relative frequency describes one specific value while cumulative relative frequency describes an entire range building up to that value.
